notes: Income Support asylum-on-arrival issue; outcome follows Shire and is clear despite anachronistic judges metadata.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum seekers denied Income Support for not claiming on arrival
key_facts: Mrs Kola and Mr Mirzajani each entered the United Kingdom clandestinely and claimed asylum on the day of arrival but not at the port of entry.
Both were refused Income Support on the basis that they were not asylum seekers within regulation 70(3A) because they had not submitted claims on arrival.
Appeals through the Income Support Tribunal and to the Social Security Commissioner failed; permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal was granted.
The claimants argued for a liberal interpretation of 'on his arrival', relying on JCWI and UN refugee convention materials.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Social Security Commissioner decisions refusing Income Support to two asylum seekers.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; neither claimant qualified as an asylum seeker under regulation 70(3A); leave to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Under regulation 70(3A) of the Income Support (General) Regulations 1987, a person who enters clandestinely and leaves the port of entry before claiming asylum has not submitted a claim on arrival; agents cannot be relied on to excuse delay unless there is clear evidence of physical duress, following Shire v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'on his arrival' in regulation 70(3A)
Whether clandestine entrants who claim asylum later on the same day qualify for Income Support
Whether Commissioner Rowland's more flexible interpretation could assist the claimants
Effect of Shire on persons acting through agents without duress
linked_authorities: Shire v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions [2003] EWCA Civ 1465
R v Secretary of State for Social Services ex parte Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants [1997] 1 WLR 275

confidence.notes: Outcome, statutory wording, and application of Shire are explicit. Source judges metadata lists anachronistic names; enrichment follows judgment text (Kennedy, Woolf CJ, Parker, Dyson LJJ).

notes: Section 459 strike-out on group structure; Sir Martin Nourse judgment is clear though source judges metadata is unreliable.

enrichment.short_title: Section 459 petition against holding company for subsidiary conduct
key_facts: Citybranch Group Ltd was a quasi-partnership holding company with wholly owned subsidiaries Citybranch Ltd and Blaneland Ltd conducting property investment.
The Gross and Rackind families each held 50% of the parent; the Rackind family presented a winding-up petition after relationship breakdown.
The Gross family responded with a section 459 petition alleging unfairly prejudicial conduct mainly in the subsidiaries, including tax obstruction, consultancy fees, and alleged misappropriation.
The Rackind family applied to strike out the petition on the basis that section 459 could not apply where only subsidiary affairs were prejudicial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal to strike out a section 459 unfair prejudice petition in a corporate group dispute.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; petition not struck out; amendment permitted; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Conduct of the affairs of a wholly owned subsidiary may, in an appropriate group structure where the holding company's directors control and represent the subsidiary, also constitute conduct of the affairs of the holding company for the purposes of section 459 Companies Act 1985; courts should look at business realities rather than a narrow legalistic view.
legal_issues: Whether section 459 applies to a holding company where prejudicial conduct occurred in subsidiaries
Whether breakdown of shareholder trust is conduct of the company's affairs
Whether prejudice to subsidiary value can prejudice parent shareholders
Appropriate test on a strike-out application

Re Norvabron Pty Ltd (No 2) (1986) 11 ACLR 279
Re Dernacourt Investments Pty Ltd (1990) 2 ACSR 553

notes: Detailed Westminster street-trading fee challenge; statutory construction and consultation adequacy are well reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Westminster street trading fees judicial review by WESTA
key_facts: Westminster proposed substantial increases to street trading charges in 2003, especially for W1/WC2 isolated pitches previously exempt from refuse collection fees.
WESTA, representing many isolated-pitch traders, challenged the July 2003 committee decision after consultation under section 22.
The council sought full cost recovery for refuse collection, cleansing, enforcement, and administration, having accumulated a street trading account deficit.
WESTA argued the council misconstrued its powers, applied 'user pays' inconsistently, and failed to disclose adequate information.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of Westminster's decision to implement revised street trading fees and charges.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the council lawfully consulted, could recover group service costs from all licence holders, and its decision was not irrational.
enrichment.ratio: Section 22(2) of the City of Westminster Act 1999 authorises recovery from licence holders as a group for services rendered to street traders collectively, including refuse collection and enforcement, even where individual traders do not use every service; 'reasonable' qualifies the valuation of group services, not each trader's personal use; differential enforcement charges for W1/WC2 are not inconsistent with abolishing the non-refuse discount.
legal_issues: Construction of section 22 charging powers under the City of Westminster Act 1999
Whether traders may be charged for refuse collection services not individually used
Adequacy of consultation information under section 22(11)
Rationality of enforcement cost apportionment and administrative cost estimates
linked_authorities: Regina v London Borough of Tower Hamlets ex parte Tower Hamlets Combined Traders Association (CO/629/93)
Regina v Manchester City Council ex parte King [1991] 89 LGR 696

notes: Section 68 challenge to SIF dishonesty finding; psychiatric evidence point analysed thoroughly.

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor's challenge to indemnity denial for dishonest report on title
key_facts: Ms Shuttari, a sole-practice solicitor, certified a report on title to Paragon Finance despite not investigating title in a transaction involving an alleged sub-sale mortgage fraud.
The Solicitors' Indemnity Fund refused cover under the dishonesty exclusion and the matter went to arbitration before Phillip Naughton QC.
The arbitrator found dishonesty in signing the report on title and refused a late adjournment to obtain psychiatric evidence about her mental state in 1991.
Ms Shuttari challenged the award under section 68, later producing a report from Dr Harris suggesting depression may have affected her appreciation of dishonesty.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 68 Arbitration Act 1996 to remit or set aside an arbitral award refusing solicitors' indemnity cover.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no serious irregularity under section 33; refusal to adjourn for expert psychiatric evidence was fair and caused no substantial injustice.
enrichment.ratio: An arbitrator acts fairly under section 33 when refusing a very late adjournment for expert evidence after cross-examination has concluded, especially where the proposed evidence is speculative and could not realistically alter a finding that the solicitor knowingly signed a report on title that any honest solicitor would recognise as dishonest; section 68 requires substantial injustice, not merely a realistic chance of a different outcome.
legal_issues: Whether refusal to adjourn for psychiatric evidence was a serious irregularity under section 68
Meaning of dishonesty in professional indemnity context after Twinsectra
Whether Dr Harris's evidence could have caused substantial injustice
Application of section 33 fair opportunity requirements in arbitration
linked_authorities: Twinsectra Ltd v Yardley [2002] 2 AC 164

confidence.notes: Section 68/33 analysis, dishonesty test, and outcome are detailed and explicit.

notes: Important CPR costs conduct principle on detailed assessment; facts and rulings are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Conduct cannot be raised on costs assessment if omitted at trial
key_facts: Mr Aaron sued fellow solicitor Mr Shelton for breach of warranty of authority, abuse of process and conspiracy over a consent order in earlier forfeiture proceedings.
After trial evidence emerged, Mr Aaron consented to dismissal and agreed to pay indemnity costs subject to detailed assessment.
On assessment Mr Aaron sought to rely on Mr Shelton's trial conduct, including lack of authority and false affidavit evidence, to reduce costs payable.
Master Simons ruled the conduct points could not be raised on assessment and limited challenges to trial bundles and fifth-day trial costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from costs judge rulings during detailed assessment of indemnity costs after consent dismissal of a solicitor misconduct claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; paying party may not raise at detailed assessment conduct that should have been raised before the judge making the costs order.
enrichment.ratio: Where a party facing a costs order considers opponent conduct should reduce costs recoverable under CPR 44.3(6), he must raise it before the judge making the order; failing to do so, he cannot reopen the same conduct on detailed assessment under CPR 44.5(3); raising core trial issues after consenting to dismissal with indemnity costs is an abuse of process.
legal_issues: Whether conduct may be raised for the first time on detailed assessment
Interaction of CPR 44.3 and CPR 44.5
Abuse of process where consent costs order followed abandoned claim
Whether inadequate trial bundles prepared by receiving party justified separate bundle costs
linked_authorities: Henderson v Henderson (1843) 3 Hare 100
Skuse v Granada Television Ltd [1994] 1 WLR 1156
Burrows v Vauxhall Motors Ltd [1998] PIQR 48
Yat Tung Investment v Dao Heng Bank [1975] AC 581

notes: Long liability-only PI appeal on brake defect and garage attendance; appellate deference to trial judge is central.

enrichment.short_title: Defective rear brake liability after pre-accident garage service
key_facts: Clare Girbash lost control of a Ford Transit van on the A303 and suffered serious head injuries in a collision; she could not give evidence at trial.
She claimed Main Line Auto Engineering failed to identify and repair a defective rear offside brake after she allegedly brought the van in for a full service two days before the accident.
Judge Hegarty QC found on the balance of probabilities that she attended the garage on 28 April 1998 and that the brake defect caused or materially contributed to the crash.
Main Line accepted that if both findings stood, it was in breach of contract and liable.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a liability-only trial finding garage negligence caused a serious road traffic accident.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; trial judge's findings on garage attendance and causation upheld; defendant ordered to pay appeal costs.
enrichment.ratio: On disputed circumstantial evidence, especially where a seriously injured claimant relies on family witness evidence, an appellate court should be slow to overturn a careful trial judge's balance-of-probabilities findings that the claimant attended for servicing shortly before the accident and that an identified brake defect materially contributed to the collision.
legal_issues: Whether the claimant proved on the balance of probabilities that she brought the van to Main Line on 28 April 1998
Whether defective rear offside brakes caused or materially contributed to the accident
Appropriate appellate restraint in reviewing judge's assessment of witness credibility
Breach of contract and liability where repair fault is established

confidence.notes: Outcome and core issues are clear though the judgment is fact-heavy and very long.

notes: EU standstill/Ankara Agreement asylum-business entry issue; Savas analysis is central and well explained.

enrichment.short_title: Turkish asylum seekers and Ankara Agreement standstill rules

statutes_considered.title: Additional Protocol to the Ankara Agreement 1973

key_facts: Two Turkish nationals, Mr Tum and Mr Dari, claimed asylum on arrival and were returnable under the Dublin Convention but later applied to remain to establish businesses.
They argued the Secretary of State should apply 1973 immigration rules under the Ankara Agreement standstill provision rather than current restrictive business rules.
Davis J allowed judicial review; the Secretary of State appealed and sought a reference to the ECJ.
Neither respondent was alleged to have entered by fraud; both had operated or sought to operate self-employed businesses while their status was unresolved.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from judicial review allowing Turkish asylum seekers to rely on 1973 immigration rules for business entry applications.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; Secretary of State applied wrong rules; leave to appeal refused; no ECJ reference required.
enrichment.ratio: The Ankara Agreement Article 41(1) standstill clause requires national courts to apply domestic immigration rules no stricter than those in force on 1 January 1973 when assessing business-establishment applications, even for Turkish nationals whose asylum claims failed and who are treated under section 11 Immigration Act 1971 as not having entered; fraud would exclude protection, but bona fide unsuccessful asylum seekers are not disqualified.
legal_issues: Whether Article 41(1) applies to Turkish asylum seekers seeking business leave
Effect of section 11 Immigration Act 1971 temporary admission on standstill rights
Proper reading of ECJ authorities in Savas and Kondova
Whether a reference to the ECJ was necessary
linked_authorities: Savas (Case C-37/98) [2000] ECR I-2927
Kondova (Case C-235/99)
Abatay and Others (Case C-317/01)

notes: Short mention judgment ordering ECJ reference on VAT single-supply/zero-rating point.

enrichment.short_title: VAT reference on zero-rated caravan single supply
key_facts: Talacre Beach Caravan Sales Ltd sold new static caravans including removable contents such as kitchens, furniture and carpets.
The manufacturer split price between caravan and contents; the retailer charged a single zero-rated price relying on Schedule 8 Group 9.
The tribunal held there was a single supply but apportioned standard-rate VAT to removable contents excluded by note (a).
Lindsay J upheld apportioned rating; on permission to appeal Chadwick LJ identified a need for ECJ guidance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Mention hearing on whether to refer questions to the European Court of Justice in a VAT second appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Question referred to the ECJ; costs of the hearing to be costs in the case; counsel to agree draft order.
enrichment.ratio: Where a member state zero-rates specified goods under an Article 28 derogation but excludes certain removable contents from zero-rating, whether a single supply precludes charging standard-rate VAT on the excluded items is a question of EU VAT law appropriate for reference to the ECJ, not merely domestic construction.
legal_issues: Whether a single supply under Card Protection Plan precludes split VAT rates on excluded items
Scope of UK zero-rating derogation for caravans under Schedule 8 Group 9
Whether note (a) removable contents can be taxed at standard rate within one supply
Appropriateness of an Article 234 ECJ reference
linked_authorities: Card Protection Plan Ltd v Commissioners of Customs and Excise [1999] STC 270

notes: Green Belt agricultural dwelling with integrated livery use; policy interpretation challenge failed.

enrichment.short_title: Green Belt mobile home for integrated farm and livery business
key_facts: High Barn Farm in Guildford Green Belt operated a mixed livestock and livery business; a mobile home was used for residential purposes in breach of planning control.
An inspector granted temporary planning permission for the mobile home, finding functional need for a full-time on-site worker and no suitable alternative accommodation.
The inspector treated the livery operation as integral to the farming enterprise when applying PPG7 Annex I and local policy RE12.
Guildford Borough Council challenged the decision as misinterpreting agricultural dwelling policies by including non-agricultural livery activities.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to an inspector's decision granting planning permission for a temporary agricultural worker dwelling.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; inspector's interpretation of PPG7, PPG2 and local policies was reasonably open; decision lawful.
enrichment.ratio: Where livery activities complement agriculture and are operated as an integral part of a single farm holding, an inspector may reasonably treat the enterprise as a whole when applying PPG7 Annex I and local agricultural dwelling policies, even though livery alone is not an agricultural use; such a pragmatic interpretation is not unlawful.
legal_issues: Whether PPG7 Annex I permits functional need assessment to include integrated livery activities
Whether a mobile home for a mixed farm/livery worker is appropriate Green Belt development under PPG2
Proper approach to interpreting planning policy guidance
Whether inspector erred by not isolating purely agricultural need
linked_authorities: R v Derbyshire County Council ex parte Woods [1997] JPL 958

confidence.notes: Policy framework, inspector findings, and Richards J's interpretation analysis are thorough and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Section 459 petition disclosure and further information orders
key_facts: Minority shareholders in Edwardian Group Ltd, a profitable hotel company, petitioned under section 459 alleging unfair prejudice through excessive remuneration paid to Singh family directors after Mr Gulhati's removal.
The company sought to participate actively in the petition to defend remuneration policy but was permanently restrained by Sir Francis Ferris from spending company funds on that participation.
The petitioners applied for disclosure of company documents about its attempted participation and financial information to assess remuneration and settlement options.
Shareholder respondents' disclosure statements signed only by Jasminder Singh were challenged as non-compliant with CPR 31.10.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory applications in an unfair prejudice petition for disclosure, further information and compliance with disclosure rules.
enrichment.outcome: Company ordered to disclose participation-related advice and specified financial documents; shareholder respondents must provide compliant individual disclosure statements; further information orders partly resolved pending petition amendment on benefits in kind.
enrichment.ratio: In section 459 proceedings a company joined as nominal respondent must disclose legal advice obtained about how to respond to the petition in the interests of all shareholders, not advice in defence of hostile shareholder litigation; shareholder respondents must each personally comply with CPR 31.10 disclosure statements; management accounts and valuations may be ordered where relevant to assessing alleged excessive director remuneration and settlement.
legal_issues: Whether company legal advice on petition participation is privileged or disclosable
Relevance of financial documents to excessive remuneration allegations
Compliance with CPR 31.10 individual disclosure statement requirements
Scope of further information on benefits in kind and quasi-partnership allegations
linked_authorities: Re Hydrosan Ltd [1991] BCLC 418
CAS (Nominees) Ltd v Nottingham Forest Plc [2001] 1 All ER 954
Gnitrow Ltd v Cape Plc [2000] 1 WLR 2327
